analysis.one_liner: Bans open-market stock buybacks by public companies and gives workers one-third of board seats.
analysis.headline: The Reward Work Act never left the House Financial Services Committee: introduced June 19, 2019 with 16 Democratic cosponsors, it received no hearing, no vote, and died when the Congress ended January 3, 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The Reward Work Act would have done two things to large public companies. First, it would ban them from buying back their own shares on the stock market — a practice companies use to push their share price up, which critics say diverts cash that could go to wages. Second, it would require that one-third of every public company's board of directors be elected directly by the company's own employees, one person one vote. The bill was sent to the House Financial Services Committee and was never heard from again.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers at public companies would gain the most: under the bill, employees would elect one-third of the board and, through SEC rules written with the National Labor Relations Board, would get a direct voice in how the company is run [S3]. Workers would also gain indirectly if companies, unable to spend on buybacks, redirected cash to pay or investment — buybacks currently run hundreds of billions of dollars a year and lift earnings-per-share, a number executive pay is often tied to. Ordinary retirement savers could benefit if companies chose dividends or wage growth instead. The Securities and Exchange Commission and national exchanges would gain new rulemaking and enforcement duties.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits any public company from purchasing its own shares on a national securities exchange, and voids SEC Rule 10b-18 — the regulation that currently shields companies from manipulation liability when they buy back stock on the open market.

Bars a company from registering its securities on a national exchange unless at least one-third of its directors are chosen by employees in a one-employee-one-vote election, giving workers direct representation at the top of the company.
Directs the SEC, in consultation with the National Labor Relations Board, to write rules making board elections fair and democratic and to seat employee representatives within two years of enactment.
Companies could still buy back shares through tender offers — direct offers to shareholders outside the open market — which the bill explicitly leaves legal, blunting the ban.

analysis.who_pays: Large publicly traded corporations and their executives would bear the cost: they would lose the open-market buyback as a tool for boosting share price and earnings-per-share, and would have to surrender one-third of board seats to employee-elected directors. Stock exchanges would lose buyback trading volume. Shareholders who favor buybacks as a way to receive cash could see returns shift toward dividends or company investment.

drawbacks.text: The buyback ban has a large loophole: the bill leaves tender offers fully legal, so a determined company could still repurchase much of its stock by making direct offers to shareholders, just outside the open market.

Economists who defend buybacks argue they return excess cash to shareholders — including pension funds and 401(k) investors — and recycle capital to more productive uses; an outright ban could reduce returns for ordinary retirement savers, not just executives.

Requiring one-third of boards to be employee-elected raises questions the bill does not resolve, such as how employee directors balance duties to workers against legal duties to all shareholders, and whether the SEC and NLRB can run fair company-wide elections across thousands of firms in two years.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The goals — curbing buybacks and giving workers a board voice — are real and the board-seat requirement is genuinely novel. But the design is leaky: the tender-offer exemption means companies could largely route around the buyback ban [S3], and the board mandate's practical details were left entirely to future rulemaking. An honest supporter would call this a strong statement of principle with unproven mechanics, not a finished fix.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it died there when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Jesús 'Chuy' García of Illinois introduced the Reward Work Act on June 19, 2019, joined on day one by 13 other House Democrats including Ro Khanna, Rashida Tlaib, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, and Ayanna Pressley.
Sixteen House Democrats ultimately signed on as cosponsors — about 7% of the 231-member Democratic caucus. No Republican cosponsored.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services the same day. The committee took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and the bill never reached the House floor.
The 116th Congress ended January 3, 2021, and the bill expired with it. A companion version was not enacted.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large public companies and their executives are better off: they keep the open-market buyback as a tool for lifting share prices and executive stock compensation, and boards remain entirely chosen by shareholders with no employee-elected seats.

for.name: Rep. Jesús 'Chuy' García
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the House floor the day it was filed.

for.name: 16 of 231 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no other action was taken on their behalf.

against.name: Maxine Waters
against.what_they_did: Her committee, which held jurisdiction over the bill, never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on it during the two-year Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 17 supporters — the sponsor and 16 cosponsors — were House Democrats, roughly 7% of the 231-member caucus; no Republican supported it, and because the bill never got a vote, no formal opposition roll call was ever recorded.

industries.industry: Large publicly traded corporations and their executives
industries.note: Executives' compensation is often tied to earnings-per-share and stock price, both of which buybacks lift; the bill would take away the open-market buyback entirely and seat employee-elected directors on every public board. In this bill the industry's interest in keeping both tools runs directly against the workers it employs.

industries.industry: Stock exchanges (NYSE, Nasdaq) and securities trading firms
industries.note: Exchanges and the trading firms that execute repurchase programs would lose a large, steady block of order flow, and both would take on new SEC-directed compliance duties. The loss to ordinary people is indirect and small by comparison.

Funds that rely on buybacks as a channel for returning cash would see payouts shift toward dividends or retained earnings; some funds would also gain influence, since removing employee-elected directors is not in play — actually their board control would be diluted by the one-third employee seats.
